error_modes.label: Break altitude control

texts.0: SP, due to an unstabilized level-off on the initial, arrived at the break point without having captured the briefed pattern altitude. Break altitude deviated beyond 300 feet and the vertical trend was allowed to continue through the roll. The IP intervened on the controls to reposition the aircraft within the break zone at the correct altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction on the initial, allowed the aircraft to drift off the briefed pattern altitude at the break point. Break altitude reached the 300 feet limit and was corrected only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP. The briefed altitude was regained late, well into the turn to downwind.
texts.2: SP, due to an attitude change applied before the power was set, allowed break altitude to leave the 150 feet band. The deviation reached approximately 250 feet before SP identified the trend on the altimeter and re-established the briefed altitude unaided. The correction was completed before roll-out on downwind.
texts.3: SP flew the break at the briefed pattern altitude with deviations held inside 150 feet throughout the roll and the deceleration. Power and pitch were coordinated at the break point so that no vertical excursion developed. Altitude control required no prompting at any stage of the break.
texts.4: SP entered and completed the break with altitude deviations that were barely readable on the altimeter. Pitch and power were set before the break point, so the roll was flown with no correction required at all.
texts.marginal: SP held break altitude within the required standard, but the deviations sat near the outer edge of the 150 feet band on every pattern and always in the climbing sense. The tendency is to allow the nose to rise as bank is applied at the break point. SP is expected to set the power reduction earlier on the initial so that altitude is captured and trimmed before the break.

texts_at.0: SP flew the break with the IP calling for the power reduction on the initial to be made in anticipation of the break, since capturing pattern altitude at the break point without that anticipation has not yet been practiced. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to anticipate the power reduction independently on the next break.
texts_at.1: SP flew the break at the briefed pattern altitude, holding the deviation to approximately 280 feet, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the power reduction on the initial being confirmed only after the vertical trend had already appeared rather than in anticipation of it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce power on the initial in anticipation of the break rather than after the trend appears.
texts_at.2: SP held break altitude within about 220 feet, due to the attitude change being applied a beat before the power was fully set rather than together with it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set power and attitude together at the break point.
texts_at.3: SP flew the break at the briefed pattern altitude within approximately 110 feet, due to the coordination of power and pitch settling a fraction after the roll began rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to coordinate power and pitch with the roll itself rather than a moment after it.

texts_above.1: SP flew the break at the briefed pattern altitude, holding the deviation to approximately 280 feet after the power reduction was called in anticipation. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP flew the break at the briefed pattern altitude on every pattern, holding the deviation to about 180 feet with power and pitch coordinated at the break point so no vertical excursion developed. Setting the power a fraction earlier on the initial would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good break-altitude discipline.
texts_above.3: SP flew the break at the briefed pattern altitude with deviations held inside 100 feet throughout the roll and the deceleration on every pattern, with altitude control needing no prompting at any stage. The only refinement available was to set the power a fraction earlier still on the initial. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good break-altitude discipline.
texts_above.4: SP entered and completed the break with altitude deviations barely readable on the altimeter on every pattern, pitch and power set before the break point so the roll needed no correction at all. The technique is already sound; nothing in the break sequencing needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent break-altitude discipline.

error_modes.label: Break bank angle

texts.0: SP, due to an aggressive roll input made without reference to the attitude indicator, exceeded the briefed break bank by more than 15 degrees. The excessive bank was not reduced as the turn progressed and produced a downwind spacing that could not be recovered. The IP took control to unload the aircraft and re-establish the briefed bank.
texts.1: SP, due to an unmonitored roll rate at the break point, applied a bank that reached the 15 degrees deviation limit from the briefed value. The bank was reduced only after the IP called the attitude, and the correct value was re-established late in the turn. Spacing on downwind had to be adjusted as a result.
texts.2: SP, due to a roll input applied faster than the briefed rate, allowed break bank to deviate past the 10 degrees band. The deviation reached approximately 13 degrees before SP cross-checked the attitude indicator and set the briefed bank without assistance. Downwind spacing was unaffected.
texts.3: SP established the briefed break bank promptly and held it within 10 degrees for the whole turn. The roll rate was smooth and the bank was cross-checked against the attitude indicator throughout, giving the planned downwind spacing.
texts.4: SP set the briefed break bank in a single smooth input and held it with deviations that were not measurable on the attitude indicator. The resulting downwind spacing matched the briefed value with no adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP kept break bank within the required standard, but the values consistently sat at the shallow edge of the 10 degrees band. The tendency is to under-bank at the break and then correct with a second input. SP is expected to establish the briefed bank in one deliberate roll and confirm it on the attitude indicator.

texts_at.0: SP rolled into the break with the IP calling the roll rate from the first movement of the stick, since monitoring that rate from the very start of the roll has not yet been practiced without that call. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to monitor the roll rate independently from the first movement on the next break.
texts_at.1: SP established the briefed break bank, holding the deviation to approximately 14 degrees, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the roll rate being monitored only after the bank had already begun to develop rather than from the first movement of the stick. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to monitor the roll rate from the first movement of the stick rather than only once the bank has developed.
texts_at.2: SP held break bank within about 12 degrees, due to the roll input being applied faster than the briefed rate before being eased back to it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the roll input at the briefed rate from the start rather than easing into it.
texts_at.3: SP established the briefed break bank within approximately 7 degrees, due to the cross-check against the attitude indicator running a fraction behind the roll rather than matching it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the attitude-indicator cross-check matched to the roll rather than a fraction behind it.

texts_above.1: SP established the briefed break bank, holding the deviation to approximately 14 degrees after the roll rate was called from the first movement. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP established the briefed break bank promptly on every pattern, holding it within about 12 degrees with the roll rate smooth and cross-checked against the attitude indicator throughout. Setting the bank in a single deliberate roll would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid break-bank control.
texts_above.3: SP established the briefed break bank promptly and held it within a few degrees for the whole turn on every pattern, with the roll rate smooth and the resulting downwind spacing matching the briefed value. The only refinement available was to confirm the bank on the attitude indicator a fraction sooner still. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate break-bank control.
texts_above.4: SP set the briefed break bank in a single smooth input on every pattern, with deviations not measurable on the attitude indicator and the resulting downwind spacing matching the briefed value exactly. The technique is already sound; nothing in the roll technique needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding break-bank control.

error_modes.label: Downwind altitude control

texts.0: SP, due to an untrimmed aircraft after the configuration change, did not level at the briefed downwind altitude. The deviation passed 300 feet and continued to develop while attention remained on the landing gear indications. The IP intervened on the controls to return the aircraft to the pattern altitude before the base turn.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed level-off after the break, allowed downwind altitude to reach the 300 feet limit. The deviation was corrected only after the IP called the altitude twice, and the pattern altitude was regained abeam the intended touchdown point. Control of the aircraft was retained by SP throughout.
texts.2: SP, due to a trim change that was not followed up after gear extension, allowed downwind altitude to leave the 150 feet band. The deviation reached approximately 230 feet before SP detected it on the altimeter and re-established the briefed altitude without prompting. The base turn was commenced at the correct altitude.
texts.3: SP levelled at the briefed downwind altitude immediately after the break and held it within 150 feet for the whole leg. The aircraft was trimmed after each configuration change so that no vertical drift developed before the base turn.
texts.4: SP held downwind altitude with deviations that were negligible on the altimeter from roll-out to the base turn. The aircraft was trimmed hands-off through both configuration changes and required no altitude correction.
texts.marginal: SP held downwind altitude within the required standard, but the deviations approached the edge of the 150 feet band each time the landing gear was extended. The tendency is to accept the pitch change instead of trimming it out. SP is expected to re-trim promptly after each configuration change so that the leg is flown without a vertical trend.

texts_at.0: SP leveled on downwind with the IP calling for the trim to be reset in the same movement as each configuration change, since re-trimming through gear and flap extension together has not yet been practiced without that call. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to re-trim in the same movement independently on the next downwind.
texts_at.1: SP levelled at the briefed downwind altitude after the break, holding the deviation to approximately 280 feet, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the trim change after gear extension being made a beat after the pitch change rather than with it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to trim in the same movement as the pitch change rather than a beat after it.
texts_at.2: SP held downwind altitude within about 220 feet, due to the trim follow-up after the second configuration change being made a fraction later than the first. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to give the trim follow-up the same priority after every configuration change.
texts_at.3: SP levelled at the briefed downwind altitude within approximately 110 feet, due to the final trim check settling a fraction after the aircraft had already stabilized rather than as it stabilized. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the final trim check as the aircraft stabilizes rather than shortly after.

texts_above.1: SP levelled at the briefed downwind altitude immediately after the break, holding it within approximately 280 feet after the trim reset was called with the configuration change. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP levelled at the briefed downwind altitude immediately after the break on every pattern, holding it within about 180 feet with the aircraft trimmed after each configuration change so no vertical drift developed. Trimming a fraction sooner after gear extension would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady downwind-altitude discipline.
texts_above.3: SP levelled at the briefed downwind altitude immediately after the break and held it within 100 feet for the whole leg on every pattern, with the aircraft trimmed hands-off after both configuration changes. The only refinement available was to trim a fraction sooner still after the second change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed downwind-altitude discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held downwind altitude with deviations negligible on the altimeter from roll-out to the base turn on every pattern, trimmed hands-off through both configuration changes with no correction required. The technique is already sound; nothing in the trim sequencing needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional downwind-altitude discipline.

error_modes.label: Downwind airspeed and minimum speed compliance

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of airspeed during the approach, allowed the aircraft to decelerate below the 120 KIAS minimum downwind airspeed, for which no negative tolerance exists. The decreasing trend was not detected and no power was added as the gear and flaps produced additional drag. The IP intervened with power to restore the briefed airspeed before the base turn.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted airspeed cross-check while attention remained on the pattern spacing, allowed downwind airspeed to reach the 20 knots upper limit of the tolerance. Power was reduced only after the IP called the airspeed, and the briefed value was regained late on the leg. The excess energy then had to be dissipated in the base turn.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting left high after the break, allowed downwind airspeed to rise outside the 10 knots band. The excess reached approximately 15 knots before SP identified it on the airspeed indicator and reset the power unaided. The briefed airspeed was established before the base turn with no assistance.
texts.3: SP established the aircraft on downwind at or above the 120 KIAS minimum and held the briefed airspeed within 10 knots on the high side, with no excursion below the minimum at any point. Power was adjusted in anticipation of each configuration change.
texts.4: SP flew the whole downwind leg with airspeed effectively on the briefed value, never below the 120 KIAS minimum and with excess speed that was not measurable. Power was led ahead of both configuration changes so that no correction was needed.
texts.marginal: SP kept downwind airspeed inside the standard, but the values were repeatedly close to the 120 KIAS minimum, where no negative tolerance is allowed. The tendency is to reduce power early and then chase the speed back. SP is expected to protect the minimum airspeed with a positive margin and to cross-check it at each configuration change.

texts_at.0: SP flew the downwind with the IP calling for power to be reset to the downwind setting the instant the break was complete, since protecting the 120 KIAS minimum, for which no negative tolerance exists, has not yet been practiced without that call. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to reset power to the downwind setting independently the instant the break is complete.
texts_at.1: SP established the aircraft on downwind at or above the 120 KIAS minimum, holding the briefed airspeed to approximately 18 knots fast, at the outer edge of the standard, due to power being left high after the break for a moment longer than the technique calls for before it was reduced. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce power to the downwind setting as soon as the break is complete rather than a moment later.
texts_at.2: SP held downwind airspeed within about 15 knots fast of the briefed value, never below the 120 KIAS minimum, due to the power reset after the break being sized correctly but applied a beat late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reset the power at the moment the break is complete rather than a beat after it.
texts_at.3: SP established the aircraft on downwind at or above the 120 KIAS minimum, holding the briefed airspeed within approximately 8 knots on the high side, due to the power anticipation for the second configuration change trailing the first by a fraction. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate both configuration changes with the same lead.

texts_above.1: SP established the aircraft on downwind at or above the 120 KIAS minimum, holding the briefed airspeed to approximately 18 knots fast after the power reset was called. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP held downwind airspeed within about 12 knots on the high side of the briefed value on every pattern, never below the 120 KIAS minimum, with power anticipated ahead of each configuration change. Resetting the power a fraction sooner after the break would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable airspeed protection.
texts_above.3: SP flew the whole downwind leg with airspeed within a few knots of the briefed value on every pattern, never below the 120 KIAS minimum, power led ahead of both configuration changes so no correction was needed. The only refinement available was to lead the power a fraction sooner still on the fastest breaks. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good airspeed protection.
texts_above.4: SP flew the whole downwind leg with airspeed effectively on the briefed value on every pattern, never below the 120 KIAS minimum and with excess speed not measurable, power led ahead of both configuration changes. The technique is already sound; nothing in the power anticipation needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior airspeed protection.

error_modes.label: Base leg airspeed control

texts.0: SP, due to a base turn commenced with the power still at the downwind setting, did not control the airspeed against the increasing bank and drag. The airspeed fell below the briefed base value, for which no negative tolerance exists, while the descent was continued. The IP intervened with power and bank to restore the briefed airspeed before the roll-out on final.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction entering the base turn, allowed base leg airspeed to reach the 20 knots upper limit of the tolerance. The airspeed was reduced only after the IP called it, and the briefed value was reached at the roll-out point rather than before it. The final was then flown with residual excess energy.
texts.2: SP, due to a descent rate established before the power was set, allowed base leg airspeed to leave the 10 knots band. The excess reached approximately 15 knots before SP recognized it and reset the power without prompting. The briefed airspeed was re-established before the roll-out onto final.
texts.3: SP flew the base leg with airspeed held within 10 knots on the high side of the briefed value and with no excursion below it. Power was set in the turn so that the aircraft arrived at the roll-out point on speed and on profile.
texts.4: SP controlled base leg airspeed with deviations that were not readable on the indicator and with no approach to the lower boundary. Power, bank and descent rate were coordinated so that the roll-out onto final needed no airspeed correction.
texts.marginal: SP held base leg airspeed within the standard, but the values sat at the upper edge of the band on each pattern. The tendency is to carry excess energy into the base turn and unload it late. SP is expected to reduce power at the start of the turn so that the briefed airspeed is stabilized before the roll-out point.

texts_at.0: SP flew the base leg with the IP calling for power to be reduced in the same movement as the roll into the turn, since protecting the base leg minimum, for which no negative tolerance exists, has not yet been practiced without that call. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to reduce power in the same movement independently on the next base turn.
texts_at.1: SP flew the base leg with airspeed held to approximately 18 knots on the high side of the briefed value and with no excursion below it, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the power reduction entering the turn being confirmed only after the bank had already increased rather than with it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce power in the same movement as rolling into the base turn.
texts_at.2: SP held base leg airspeed within about 15 knots on the high side, due to the descent rate being established a beat before power was fully set rather than together with it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set power and descent rate together entering the base turn.
texts_at.3: SP flew the base leg with airspeed held within approximately 8 knots on the high side of the briefed value, due to the roll-out point being anticipated a fraction later than the technique calls for. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate the roll-out point a little earlier in the turn.

texts_above.1: SP flew the base leg with airspeed held to approximately 18 knots on the high side of the briefed value and with no excursion below it, after the power reduction was called with the roll-in. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP flew the base leg with airspeed held within about 12 knots on the high side on every pattern, and with no excursion below the briefed value, power set in the turn so the roll-out point arrived on speed and on profile. Setting power a fraction earlier entering the turn would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound base-leg discipline.
texts_above.3: SP controlled base leg airspeed with deviations within a few knots of the briefed value on every pattern and with no approach to the lower boundary, power, bank and descent rate coordinated so the roll-out needed no airspeed correction. The only refinement available was to coordinate the descent rate a fraction sooner still. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed base-leg discipline.
texts_above.4: SP controlled base leg airspeed with deviations not readable on the indicator on every pattern and with no approach to the lower boundary, power, bank and descent rate coordinated so the roll-out onto final needed no airspeed correction at all. The technique is already sound; nothing in the base-leg coordination needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional base-leg discipline.

error_modes.label: Final altitude and glidepath

texts.0: SP, due to a roll-out completed inside the briefed roll-out point, arrived on final below the required glidepath. The altitude deviation passed the 100 feet low limit and the descent was continued without any power addition. The IP intervened on the controls to arrest the sink and re-establish the aircraft on the correct final profile.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent rate that was not adjusted after roll-out on final, allowed final altitude to reach the tolerance limit, 200 feet high or 100 feet low. The profile was corrected only after the IP called the deviation, and the aircraft regained the glidepath late on final. The correction was made with SP still flying the aircraft.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting that lagged the pitch change on final, allowed the altitude to leave the tight band of 100 feet high and 50 feet low. The deviation reached approximately 150 feet high before SP recognized the profile error and corrected it unaided, re-establishing the glidepath well before the threshold.
texts.3: SP flew the final within 100 feet high and 50 feet low of the correct profile from roll-out to the threshold. Pitch and power were coordinated so that the glidepath was stabilized early and no large correction was required.
texts.4: SP tracked the final glidepath with altitude deviations that were negligible against the asymmetric tolerance and with no tendency toward the low side. The profile was stabilized at roll-out and flown to the threshold without correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept the final within the required altitude tolerance, but the profile was consistently near the low edge of the band, where the allowance is only 50 feet. The tendency is to establish the descent before the power is reduced and to correct with pitch alone. SP is expected to fly the final slightly above the tight band and to protect the low side with early power.

texts_at.0: SP flew the final with the IP calling for the descent rate to be adjusted the instant roll-out was complete, since stabilizing the profile at roll-out itself has not yet been practiced without that call. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to adjust the descent rate at roll-out independently on the next final.
texts_at.1: SP flew the final within the tolerance limit, holding the profile to approximately 180 feet high, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the descent rate after roll-out being adjusted only once the profile had already drifted rather than as roll-out was completed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to adjust the descent rate at roll-out itself rather than once the profile has already drifted.
texts_at.2: SP held the final profile to about 150 feet high, outside the tight band but inside the tolerance limit, due to the power setting lagging the pitch change by a beat rather than matching it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring the power setting into the same instant as the pitch change on final.
texts_at.3: SP flew the final within 100 feet high and 50 feet low of the correct profile, holding the deviation to approximately 80 feet high, due to the profile being stabilized a fraction after roll-out rather than at roll-out itself. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to stabilize the profile at roll-out itself rather than a fraction after it.

texts_above.1: SP flew the final within the tolerance limit, holding the profile to approximately 180 feet high after the descent rate adjustment was called at roll-out. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP tracked the final glidepath within about 130 feet high of the correct profile on every approach, pitch and power coordinated so no large correction was required and the glidepath stabilized early. Coordinating pitch and power a fraction sooner at roll-out would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady glidepath control.
texts_above.3: SP flew the final within a comfortable margin of the correct profile on every approach, the glidepath stabilized early with pitch and power coordinated from roll-out to the threshold. The only refinement available was to stabilize the profile a fraction sooner still on the steepest roll-outs. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise glidepath control.
texts_above.4: SP tracked the final glidepath with deviations negligible against the asymmetric tolerance and with no tendency toward the low side on every approach, the profile stabilized at roll-out and flown to the threshold without correction. The technique is already sound; nothing in the profile management needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate glidepath control.

error_modes.label: AOA units through downwind, base and final (AOA pattern)
error_modes.source: specific:DOWN WIND - BASE - FINAL / AOA UNITS

texts.0: SP, due to an AOA pattern flown on airspeed references instead of the AOA indexer, did not control the angle of attack through the base turn. The AOA deviated by more than 3 units and the aircraft was allowed to approach the stall warning regime in the turn. The IP intervened on the controls to unload the aircraft and re-establish the briefed AOA.
texts.1: SP, due to an AOA cross-check that was made only intermittently, allowed the AOA to reach the 3 unit deviation limit on base and final. The angle of attack was reduced only after the IP called the indexer indication, and the briefed value was re-established late on final. No stall characteristics developed.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch input applied faster than the indexer response, allowed the AOA to leave the 1.5 unit band during the base turn. error_modes.label: AOA pattern: configuration timing and pitch for AOA, power for glidepath

texts.0: SP, due to configuring too late to be at optimum AOA with a stabilized power setting by the perch, flew the AOA pattern chasing the indexer through the final turn. The angle of attack deviated more than 3 units from the on-speed donut and the power was then reduced as early and as quickly as in a normal pattern, producing a high sink rate at a slower than normal approach speed. The IP intervened with power and pitch to recover the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to flaps lowered well after the gear and only close to the perch, entered the final turn without a stabilized power setting. The angle of attack reached the 3 units deviation from the on-speed indication and was returned to the donut only after the IP called the indexer. Power was also reduced too early in the roundout, leaving the sink rate higher than normal.
texts.2: SP, due to the AOA technique being reversed after roll-out, corrected the indication with power and the glidepath with pitch, and let the angle of attack leave the 1.5 units band and reach approximately 2.5 units above the donut. SP identified the reversal without prompting, used pitch to set the optimum AOA and power to control the rate of descent, and re-established the on-speed indication before the threshold.
texts.3: SP lowered the flaps after the landing gear on downwind and was at optimum AOA with a stabilized power setting by the perch, holding the on-speed donut within 1.5 units through the final turn and final. Pitch was used to maintain the AOA and power to control the rate of descent throughout.
texts.4: SP configured early enough that the aircraft was on the donut and stabilized well before the perch, and the on-speed indication was held with corrections too small to register on the AOA gauge. The final approach power setting was carried into the roundout as required rather than reduced at the normal pattern point.
texts.marginal: SP flew the AOA pattern within the standard, but the configuration was completed only just before the perch and the indexer sat at the slow edge of the band during the final turn. The tendency is to correct the angle of attack with power instead of pitch. SP is expected to lower the flaps immediately after the landing gear on downwind and to use pitch for AOA and power for the rate of descent.
